stem: Which of the following is a recognized cause of Menkes disease?
rationale: Menkes disease is associated with copper deficiency.
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > BIOMEDICAL IMPORTANCE

stem: In which structure is calcium primarily found?
rationale: Calcium contributes approximately 2% of the human body mass, primarily contained in bones, teeth, and cartilage. The remaining 0.4 to 0.5% of the human body mass is accounted for by numerous inorganic elements.
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > BIOMEDICAL IMPORTANCE > Humans Require Minute Quantities of Several Inorganic Elements

stem: Which substance is required for the synthesis of tetraiodothyronine?
rationale: Iodine is required for the synthesis of tri- and tetraiodothyronine. Selenium is required for the synthesis of the amino acid selenocysteine.
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > BIOMEDICAL IMPORTANCE > Humans Require Minute Quantities of Several Inorganic Elements

stem: Which substance is required for the synthesis of the amino acid selenocysteine?
rationale: Selenium is required for the synthesis of the amino acid selenocysteine. Vitamins are essential for health and are covered in Chapter 44.
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > BIOMEDICAL IMPORTANCE > Humans Require Minute Quantities of Several Inorganic Elements

stem: Which substance is required by ribonucleotide reductase?
rationale: Iron can be displaced by gallium in ribonucleotide reductase and Fe, Cu superoxide dismutase.
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > TOXICITY OF HEAVY METALS > Displacement of an Essential Cation

stem: Which substance is required by superoxide dismutase?
rationale: Iron can be displaced by gallium in ribonucleotide reductase and Fe, Cu superoxide dismutase.
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > TOXICITY OF HEAVY METALS > Displacement of an Essential Cation

stem: Which agent is used in the management of heavy metal toxicity?
rationale: Acute heavy metal poisoning is treated by ingestion of chelating agents, the administration of diuretics along with the ingestion of water, or hemodialysis.
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals

stem: Which substance is required for the hydrolysis of urea?
rationale: The hydrolysis of urea requires the cooperative action of two active site Ni atoms (Figure 10–4).
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > TOXICITY OF TRANSITION METALS > Complexation Enhances Solubility & Controls Reactivity of Transition Metal Ions

stem: Which substance is synthesized by cytochrome oxidase?
rationale: Cytochrome c and myoglobin are small, 12 to 17 kDa, monomeric proteins that contain a single heme iron.
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > TOXICITY OF TRANSITION METALS > Adjacent Ligands Can Modify Redox Potential

stem: Which substrate does superoxide dismutase act on?
rationale: Superoxide dismutases (SODs) illustrate how complexation can adapt different transition metals as catalysts for a common chemical reaction.
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > TOXICITY OF TRANSITION METALS > Adjacent Ligands Can Modify Redox Potential

stem: Which substance is transported by hemerythrin in marine invertebrates?
rationale: In marine invertebrates, the iron present in the diiron center of hemerythrin can bind and transport oxygen (Figure 10–5).
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > TOXICITY OF TRANSITION METALS > Iron

stem: Methane is converted into which substance by methane monooxygenase?
rationale: Methane monooxygenase uses a similar diiron center for the oxidation of methane to methanol. This is a powerful oxidant that participates in the reduction and neutralization of a broad range of xenobiotics.
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > TOXICITY OF TRANSITION METALS > Roles of Iron in Redox Reactions

stem: Isocitrate dehydrogenase acts on which substrate in the TCA cycle?
rationale: Manganese-containing enzymes include isocitrate dehydrogenase from the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle.
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > TOXICITY OF TRANSITION METALS > Manganese

stem: Mn-catalase acts on which substrate in redox reactions?
rationale: Mn-catalase is also an example of an enzyme using Mn in redox reactions.
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > TOXICITY OF TRANSITION METALS > Manganese

stem: Tyrosinase acts on which substrate?
rationale: Tyrosinase is the first and rate-limiting step in the synthesis of melanin. Dopamine β-hydroxylase is a member of the type 3 family of copper proteins.
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > TOXICITY OF TRANSITION METALS > Copper

stem: Lysyl oxidase converts which substance in collagen or elastin?
rationale: Lysyl oxidase converts the ε-NH2 groups on some lysine side chains in collagen or elastin to aldehydes.
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > TOXICITY OF TRANSITION METALS > Copper

stem: Urease requires which substance as a key component?
rationale: Nickel is a key component of urease.
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > TOXICITY OF TRANSITION METALS > Nickel

stem: Xanthine oxidase acts on which substrate?
rationale: Xanthine oxidase catalyzes the final two oxidative steps in the pathway by which uric acid is synthesized from purine nucleotides. The oxidation of hypoxanthine to xanthine is one of these steps. The oxidation of xanthine to uric acid is the other step.
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > TOXICITY OF TRANSITION METALS > Catalytic Roles of Molybdopterin

stem: Hypoxanthine is converted into which substance?
rationale: The oxidation of hypoxanthine to xanthine is one of these steps. The oxidation of xanthine to uric acid is the other step.
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > TOXICITY OF TRANSITION METALS > Catalytic Roles of Molybdopterin

stem: Xanthine is converted into which substance by xanthine oxidase?
rationale: The oxidation of xanthine to uric acid is the other step. The bound Mo atom in these enzymes cycles among +4, +5, and +6 valence states.
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > TOXICITY OF TRANSITION METALS > Catalytic Roles of Molybdopterin

stem: Which substance is required by xanthine oxidase?
rationale: Xanthine oxidase also contains flavin. Xanthine oxidase catalyzes the final two oxidative steps in the pathway by which uric acid is synthesized from purine nucleotides.
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > TOXICITY OF TRANSITION METALS > Catalytic Roles of Molybdopterin

stem: Which substance is required by molybdopterin?
rationale: MOCS1, MOCS2, or GPNH encode proteins that catalyze key steps in the synthesis of molybdopterin. Sulfite oxidase deficiency is an autosomal inherited inborn error of metabolism.
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > TOXICITY OF TRANSITION METALS > Iron & Molybdenum Metalloenzymes

stem: Which substrate does duodenal cytochrome b act on?
rationale: This reaction is catalyzed by duodenal cytochrome b (Dcytb), a ferric reductase located on the apical membrane surface of enterocytes.
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > TOXICITY OF TRANSITION METALS > Transition Metals Are Absorbed by Diverse Mechanisms

stem: Which of the following is a recognized cause of anemia?
rationale: Excess levels of Zn can inhibit Cu absorption, which can lead to a potentially lethal anemia.
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > TOXICITY OF TRANSITION METALS > Transition Metals Are Absorbed by Diverse Mechanisms

stem: Cubilin receptors are found within which structure?
rationale: The cobalamin-intrinsic factor complex is recognized and internalized by cubilin receptors on the surface of intestinal epithelial cells.
citation: chapter_10_the_biochemical_roles_of_transition_metals — The Biochemical Roles of Transition Metals > TOXICITY OF TRANSITION METALS > Transition Metals Are Absorbed by Diverse Mechanisms
